nameStory: The fox grape gets its name from the distinctive 'foxy' flavor of its fruits - a unique musky, wild taste that early settlers found quite different from European grapes. This 'foxy' flavor became the signature taste Americans know and love in Concord grape juice, jelly, and candy, giving our native grape its wild reputation.
description: Fox grape is a vigorous climbing vine native to eastern North America that can scramble high into trees or sprawl along the ground. It produces the familiar dark purple grapes that taste like Concord grape juice - because Concord grapes are actually a cultivated variety of this wild species! The vine has large, heart-shaped leaves and can grow quite extensively, often forming dense tangles in sunny spots along forest edges.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dark purple grapes with that familiar 'Concord grape' flavor and amazing 'slip-skin' - squeeze one gently and the skin slides right off instead of crushing the pulp inside, leaving you with a peeled grape

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, heart-shaped leaves with fuzzy, whitish undersides that feel soft and woolly to the touch - run your finger along the bottom and you'll feel the dense, cottony fuzz

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Climbing vine with curly tendrils that spiral around supports - look for tendrils at every single node (joint) along the stem, which is unusual among grapes

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, greenish flowers in dense, pyramid-shaped clusters that smell sweetly fragrant on warm days in late spring to early summer

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Older stems develop shreddy, peeling bark that comes off in long strips, revealing smooth bark underneath

habitat: Fox grapes thrive in sunny to partially shaded areas along forest edges, old fields, and stream banks throughout New England. They love climbing up trees and fences, or sprawling over stone walls and rocky areas. You'll often find them in disturbed soils and areas with good drainage, from sea level up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green and fuzzy, followed by small clusters of sweetly fragrant greenish flowers in late spring. The distinctive heart-shaped leaves with woolly undersides are easy to spot as they unfurl.
seasonality.summer: Leaves are full-sized and deep green, with clusters of hard green grapes developing. The curly tendrils are actively grabbing onto supports, and the vine may be growing several feet in a season.
seasonality.fall: Grapes ripen to deep purple with that classic Concord grape flavor and slip-skin texture. Leaves turn golden yellow before dropping, and this is prime time for grape harvesting.
seasonality.winter: Bare vines show the characteristic shreddy, peeling bark on older stems. The woody vine structure and persistent grape clusters (if any remain) help with identification.

funFact: Every time you taste grape-flavored candy, soda, or jelly, you're experiencing the flavor of this wild New England vine - not European wine grapes! The fox grape is the parent of Concord grapes and dozens of other American varieties, and its genes are even in Kyoho, the world's most planted grape variety.
confusionNotes: Fox grape is most easily confused with other native grapes like riverbank grape, but fox grape's woolly white leaf undersides and slip-skin fruits are distinctive. Remember: if it tastes like Concord grape juice and the skin slips off easily, you've found a fox grape!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'fox grape,' this species has nothing to do with foxes eating it more than other animals. The name refers purely to the distinctive 'foxy' musky flavor that makes these grapes taste so different from European wine grapes. This native species revolutionized American grape growing and gave us our distinctly American grape flavor profile.
compareHints: Among New England's native grapes, fox grape stands out with its woolly white leaf undersides and slip-skin fruits. Riverbank grape has smooth leaf undersides and doesn't have the slip-skin feature, while summer grape has more deeply lobed leaves. The tendrils-at-every-node feature helps distinguish fox grape from most other climbing vines in the region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild grapes, riverbank grape has the smallest, most tart fruit and the strongest preference for wet areas.
Summer grape stands out from other New England grapes primarily by its habitat preference for dry uplands rather than moist areas.

Wine grapes differ from native New England grapes primarily in their fruit - the clusters are much denser and tighter, and the individual grapes are noticeably sweeter with less of the tart, 'foxy' flavor characteristic of native species like fox grape.
Among New England's wild grapes, frost grape is distinguished by its reddish tendrils and the dramatic taste change after frost.

Among New England's wild grapes, catbird grape stands out for its deeply hand-shaped leaves with 3-5 distinct lobes, unlike fox grape's heart-shaped leaves or riverbank grape's more shallowly-lobed foliage.
Among New England's wild grapes, graybark grape stands out for its uniquely dull, wrinkled leaves that feel soft and flabby rather than firm.
